stem: http_request_duration_seconds is a classic histogram. Which expression gives the 90th percentile over the last 10 minutes?

options.note: Right. Rate the _bucket series over the window, then estimate the quantile.
φ is between 0 and 1, so the 90th percentile is 0.9.
Without rate() you'd use cumulative counts since process start, not the last 10 minutes.
quantile works across series values. It doesn't read buckets, and _sum holds no distribution.

explanation: The docs' example: histogram_quantile(0.9, rate(http_request_duration_seconds_bucket[10m])). Use rate() to set the window.
hint: Which series carry the bucket counts, and what sets the time window?

stem: You want the 90th percentile per job from a classic histogram. Which expression is correct?

options.note: Right. Keep le in the by clause so buckets stay distinct.
Dropping le merges every bucket together, so histogram_quantile can't work.
Summing per-instance percentiles isn't a valid way to combine them.
Rate first, then sum. Summing raw counters first breaks counter-reset handling.

explanation: Since the le label is required by histogram_quantile() for classic histograms, it has to be included in the by clause when aggregating.
hint: Which label tells histogram_quantile which bucket is which?

stem: To aggregate all classic histograms into one overall 95th percentile, which by clause do you use?

options.note: Right. Keep only le, so all instances are added together bucket by bucket.
That keeps instances separate and loses the bucket boundaries.
That removes le, exactly the label you must keep.
histogram_quantile calculates per label combination. You must sum explicitly to aggregate.

explanation: To aggregate all classic histograms, specify only the le label: histogram_quantile(0.9, sum by (le) (rate(x_bucket[10m]))).
hint: Keep the one label histogram_quantile needs.

stem: How do you calculate the average request duration over 5 minutes from a classic histogram or summary?

options.note: Right. Rate of the sum divided by rate of the count.
That's the average since process start, not over the last 5 minutes.
That averages the running total, which isn't the average duration.
That's the median, a different statistic from the mean.

explanation: Take a rate over the desired window, then divide the rate of the sum by the rate of the count.
hint: Average = total time ÷ number of requests, both over the same window.

sources.title: Histograms and summaries › Count and sum of observations

stem: What does rate(http_request_duration_seconds_count[5m]) on its own give you?

options.text: The number of requests per second over the last 5 minutes
options.note: Right. The _count series behaves exactly like a request counter.
That needs _sum divided by _count.
_count counts observations, not buckets.
Percentiles come from histogram_quantile.

explanation: The denominator of the average expression is useful on its own: it's the requests per second served over the window. The _count series behaves like a counter for requests.
hint: _count counts every observation, and every request is an observation.

sources.title: Histograms and summaries › Count and sum of observations

stem: Which expression calculates the fraction of requests served within 300 ms per job, using a classic histogram?

options.note: Right. The 0.3 bucket counts everything ≤ 300 ms. Divide by the total.
Use base units: 300 ms is 0.3 seconds.
That's the 30th percentile duration, not the fraction under 300 ms.
That's the average duration.

explanation: Classic case: sum by (job) (rate(x_bucket{le="0.3"}[5m])) / sum by (job) (rate(x_count[5m])). This strictly requires a bucket boundary at 0.3.
hint: Buckets are cumulative, and durations are in seconds.

stem: Your classic histogram has buckets at 0.1, 0.2, 0.5 and +Inf. You query the rate of the le="0.3" bucket. What happens?

options.text: No result is returned, because there's no bucket at 0.3 and no interpolation is applied
options.note: Right. Selecting le="0.3" needs that exact bucket to exist.

options.text: Prometheus interpolates between the 0.2 and 0.5 buckets
options.note: Interpolation happens inside histogram_quantile, not when you select a bucket directly.
There's no automatic substitution.

options.text: It errors and stops all queries
options.note: You simply get an empty result.

explanation: The classic-histogram fraction expression strictly requires a bucket boundary at 0.3. Without one, no result is returned at all.
hint: A label matcher is an exact match.

stem: Why is avg(http_request_duration_seconds{quantile="0.95"}) across replicas a bad idea?

options.text: Averaging pre-calculated quantiles gives statistically meaningless values
options.note: Right. Summaries' quantiles can't be aggregated.
PromQL will run it. The result just isn't meaningful.
Performance isn't the issue. Correctness is.
quantile is the normal label summaries use.

explanation: Aggregating precomputed quantiles from a summary rarely makes sense. Averaging them yields statistically nonsensical values. Use histograms and histogram_quantile to aggregate.
hint: Can you average medians to get the overall median?

stem: Which statements about histograms vs summaries are true? Select all that apply.

options.text: Histogram quantiles are calculated on the Prometheus server
options.note: Right. histogram_quantile does it at query time.

options.text: Summary quantiles and sliding windows must be chosen at instrumentation time
options.note: Right. They can't be recalculated later.

options.text: Histograms can be aggregated across instances
options.note: Right. Bucket counts add up.

options.text: Summary observations are cheaper than histogram observations
options.note: The reverse. Summaries do streaming quantile calculation, which is relatively expensive.

explanation: Summaries calculate streaming quantiles in the client and are relatively expensive per observation. Histograms just increment counters, and quantiles are calculated server-side and are aggregatable.
hint: Check the comparison table in the docs.

stem: With a classic histogram, the requested quantile falls into the highest (+Inf) bucket. What does histogram_quantile return?

options.text: The upper bound of the second-highest bucket
options.note: Right. It can't interpolate into infinity, so it returns that bound.
It returns the second-highest bucket's upper bound, not infinity.
NaN is for cases such as fewer than two buckets or zero observations.
No averaging is involved.

explanation: If a quantile is located in the highest bucket, the upper bound of the second-highest bucket is returned.
hint: It falls back to the largest finite bound.

stem: Almost all requests take about 220 ms, and your classic histogram's relevant bucket is 0.2 to 0.3 seconds. Why might histogram_quantile(0.95, …) report about 295 ms?

options.text: It assumes observations are spread evenly within the bucket (linear interpolation), so the error is limited by the bucket width
options.note: Right. That's exactly the example in the docs.

options.text: It always rounds up to the next bucket boundary
options.note: It interpolates. It doesn't round.
rate doesn't change observation values.

options.text: Summaries would report the same error
options.note: A summary would be very accurate here. The trade-off is that summaries can't be aggregated.

explanation: For classic histograms, histogram_quantile assumes a uniform distribution within the bucket. With a 200 to 300 ms bucket the true value could be anywhere in that range, and the docs' example estimates 295 ms for a true value near 220 ms.
hint: What does the function assume about where observations sit inside a bucket?

sources.title: Histograms and summaries › Errors of quantile estimation

stem: According to the docs' rules of thumb, when should you consider a summary?

options.note: Right. Summaries give accurate quantiles cheaply, but they can't be aggregated and are fixed at instrumentation time.

options.text: Whenever you need percentiles across many replicas
options.note: That's exactly when you need histograms.

options.text: When you want to change percentiles later in queries
options.note: Summaries fix the percentiles at instrumentation time.

options.text: Always, because they're the most efficient option
options.note: The docs put summaries last in their rules of thumb.

explanation: Rules of thumb: use native histograms if available; if you need aggregation without them, use classic histograms; only if aggregation isn't needed should you consider summaries.
hint: What is the one thing summaries can't do?

sources.title: Histograms and summaries › Errors of quantile estimation

stem: With a native histogram named http_request_duration_seconds, how does the 90th percentile query change compared with the classic form?

options.note: Right. A native histogram is a single series with composite samples, so there's no _bucket series and no le.
There's no _native suffix.

options.text: It isn't possible. Native histograms don't support quantiles
options.note: histogram_quantile works on both classic and native histograms.
histogram_quantile remains the function to use.

explanation: For a native histogram, use histogram_quantile(0.9, rate(http_request_duration_seconds[10m])). When aggregating, there's no need to keep le.
hint: Native histograms keep all buckets in one series.
